content: Biopotency is quantified in International Toxic Units (ITU) per milligram of product. Currently, there are two internationally recognized reference powders used to determine biopotency through bioassays involving bacterial preparations tested on mosquito larvae. These reference powders are used in conjunction with specific methods. The biopotency of products based on Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. israelensis (Bti) is compared to a lyophilized reference powder (IPS 82, strain 1884) of this bacterial species. This comparison is conducted using early fourth-instar larvae of Aedes aegypti (strain Bora Bora). The IPS 82 reference powder has an assigned toxicity of 15,000 ITU/mg against this insect strain. Similarly, the biopotency of products based on Bacillus sphaericus (Bsph) is determined using a lyophilized reference powder (SPH 88, strain 2362) and early fourth-instar larvae of Culex pipiens pipiens (strain Montpellier). The SPH 88 reference powder has an assigned toxicity of 1,700 ITU/mg against this insect strain. The toxicity of all bacterial preparations based on Bti or Bsph can be determined using these standard powders. The toxicity (ITU/mg) of tested products is calculated using the formula: Titer (ITU/mg) of tested product = Titer standard (ITU/mg) × LC50 (mg/L) standard ÷ LC50 (mg/L) unknown. The use of alternative bacterial larvicide reference powders or mosquito strains in these tests should be approached cautiously, as different results may arise. Any alternatives must undergo careful cross-calibration against the reference powders and strains mentioned above. Ideally, this cross-calibration should be conducted by independent expert laboratories, and the data supporting these alternatives should be made available for verification. Weigh 1 mg of the reference standard powder and transfer it to a 200 mL beaker containing 100 mL of deionized water. Add 2 mg of wetting agent, place the beaker in an ice bath, and stir or blend the mixture for 2 minutes. Check for any remaining large particulates and repeat stirring if necessary. Transfer the suspension to a 500 mL bottle, rinse the beaker and stirrer thoroughly, and add deionized water to make the total weight 500 g (500 mL). Shake the bottle vigorously to mix the contents. Confirm under a microscope that no aggregates of spores or crystals remain. If aggregates are present, further stirring or blending in the ice bath is required. This primary suspension contains 1 mg/10 mL and must be shaken vigorously before removing aliquots. Transfer 10 mL aliquots of the primary suspension into clean 12 mL tubes, which should be capped immediately. If multiple aliquots are being transferred, shake the primary suspension every 3 minutes to prevent sedimentation of spores and crystals. These aliquots can be stored for one month at 4°C or for two years in a freezer at -18°C. Each aliquot contains 1 mg of standard powder. To prepare a stock solution, transfer one 10 mL aliquot into a 100 mL bottle, rinse it twice with deionized water, and fill to a total of 100 g. Shake vigorously to produce a homogeneous suspension. Frozen aliquots must be thoroughly homogenized before use, as particles may agglomerate during freezing. The stock solution contains 10 mg/L. Subsequent dilutions are prepared directly in plastic cups containing 150 mL of deionized water. Add 25 early fourth-instar larvae of Aedes aegypti or Culex pipiens (depending on the bacterial species being tested) to each cup using a Pasteur pipette before adding bacterial suspensions. Adjust the water volume to maintain consistency. Four replicate cups are used for each concentration, along with one control cup containing only 150 mL of deionized water. For bioassays of dry products with unknown toxicity, prepare initial suspensions in the same manner as for the reference standard powder. However, replicate determinations must be made on dilutions prepared by weighing separate test portions of the product. For liquid formulations, weigh 100 mg instead of 50 mg to prepare a stock solution corresponding to 20 mg/L. Perform range-finding bioassays using a wide range of product concentrations to estimate approximate toxicity, then refine the range for a more precise bioassay. Toxicity is determined by observing mortality at 24 and 48 hours. For Bti, mortality is typically recorded at 24 hours due to its rapid action, while for Bsph, mortality is recorded at 48 hours due to its slower action. Tests with control mortality exceeding 5% or pupation rates above 5% are invalid. Mortality-concentration regression lines should ideally be calculated using statistical programs such as SAS, which incorporate Log Probit Analysis. The toxicity of an unknown preparation is determined by comparing its LC50 to that of the reference standard using the formula provided earlier. A test series is valid if the relative standard deviation (RSD) is less than 25%. Early fourth-instar larvae are used for testing as they represent the sensitivity of the target population and are convenient to handle. Homogeneous populations of early fourth-instar larvae are obtained within five days of hatching using standardized rearing methods. For Aedes aegypti, eggs are laid on filter paper, dried, and stored until needed. When larvae are required, the paper is immersed in dechlorinated water, and larval feed is added 24 hours prior to hatching to synchronize the process. For Culex pipiens pipiens, obtaining homogeneous populations is more challenging, requiring large numbers of egg rafts collected on the same day. These are stored at 15–18°C to accumulate more eggs for hatching. Early fourth-instar larvae suitable for testing are typically obtained within 7–9 days. Microbial larvicides should be stored at cool temperatures, ideally not exceeding 15°C, and retested if stored for more than one year. Accelerated storage stability tests are recommended for rapid checks on product stability. Biopotency loss should not exceed 10% below the labeled value when stored at 5°C for two years or at 15°C for one year.
